I always focus on diagnosing and recommending the best treatment plan for the child, and I defer detailed financial coordination to the practice’s administrative team.
I always ensure that all procedures requiring special consent have the correct consent form completed, signed, and documented in the patient chart before treatment begins.
I always review our parental separation policy for oral sedation and general anesthesia during the treatment planning appointment so parents are not surprised on the day of treatment.

competency_name: Treatment Planning for Long Term Health
text: I always provide exceptionally thorough evaluations and definitive treatment planning for patients facing significant barriers to care (geographic, financial or otherwise), recognizing that each visit may represent a rare opportunity to improve their oral health.

competency_name: Treatment Planning for Long Term Health
text: I always include an indirect pulp cap (IPC) in the treatment plan when a lesion approximates the pulp and pulp protection may be needed.

competency_name: Treatment Planning for Long Term Health
text: I always adhere to the AAPD Maximum Recommended Dose (MRD) and weight-based dosing guidelines for all oral sedation medications and never exceed these limits.
I always review patient notes and appointment details before starting the check-in process.
description: Knowing what's in a patient's notes before they arrive lets you anticipate needs, flag anything unusual to the clinical team, and avoid being caught off guard at the desk.
intervention_text: Think about the last time something caught you off guard at check-in — a medical alert, an outstanding balance, a patient preference. Reviewing notes in advance is what prevents those moments.

text: I always inform the clinical team of any outstanding or expected patient balances before the patient is seated.
description: Giving the clinical team a heads-up about outstanding balances means nothing comes as a surprise, and financial conversations stay at the front desk where they belong.
intervention_text: If this slipped, the clinical team may have been caught off guard in the surgery. Build this into your check-in routine before your next shift.

text: I always let new patients know at check-in that their dental nurse will collect them for a brief scan before they meet the dentist.
description: New patients who understand the flow of their appointment feel more in control and arrive at the chair with fewer anxieties — and fewer questions for the clinical team.
intervention_text: First impressions matter most with new patients. A quick, clear preview of what to expect sets the whole appointment up well — try scripting this so it comes naturally.

text: I always contact patients on the short-notice list daily, prioritising same-day and next-day open slots.
description: Consistently working the short-notice list keeps the diary full and reduces lost revenue from last-minute cancellations.
intervention_text: An empty slot costs the practice real money. Even one call a day to the short-notice list makes a measurable difference — what's getting in the way of making it happen?

text: I always communicate individually with all patients in the waiting area when we are running more than 10 minutes behind schedule.
description: Patients who are kept informed feel respected even when things aren't running to time — silence breeds frustration, a quick update builds trust.
intervention_text: Think about the last time a patient looked frustrated in the waiting area. A brief, honest update takes 20 seconds and changes the mood entirely. Make it a habit.

text: I always offer same-day emergency patients a specific appointment time when available, or a sit-and-wait option with clear expectations about wait time.
description: Emergency patients are already stressed — giving them clarity about their options and realistic expectations prevents conflict and builds loyalty.
intervention_text: Emergency patients left uncertain about whether they'll be seen tend to escalate. Giving a clear answer, even if the wait is long, keeps everyone calmer. Review how you're handling these calls.

text: I can list all common dental procedures and their typical durations from memory.
description: Confident, accurate scheduling starts with knowing your procedures — a receptionist who can recall timings from memory earns trust from both patients and the clinical team.
intervention_text: Spend 10 minutes this week going through the procedure list in CareStack. Being able to recall durations quickly makes every booking call noticeably smoother.

text: I can summarise the basic steps for all common clinical procedures when a patient asks.
description: Patients who understand what a procedure involves are more likely to accept it — a receptionist who can explain it simply and confidently is a key part of the case acceptance chain.
intervention_text: You don't need to be a clinician to explain a filling or a scale and polish. Identify the two or three procedures you're least confident describing and focus on those first.

text: I always offer relevant branded treatment literature to patients at check-out, particularly those who are undecided about a recommended treatment.
description: Leaving a patient with something tangible to read keeps the treatment conversation alive and reduces the chance of a warm lead going cold before their next visit.
intervention_text: If a patient walked out undecided and without literature, the practice has likely lost that treatment. Make sure the right brochures are stocked at your station and visible at check-out.

text: I always alert the clinical team immediately after completing patient check-in.
description: The clinical team can only run on time if they know a patient is ready — a delay in alerting them is a delay absorbed by every appointment that follows.
intervention_text: Even a 2-minute lag between check-in and alerting the team can throw the diary off. Review how you're currently signalling patient readiness and whether there's a faster method.

text: I always notify the Lead Dental Nurse if a patient has been waiting for longer than 10 minutes after check-in.
description: Proactively flagging delays keeps the clinical team accountable for patient flow and prevents a patient from feeling invisible in the waiting area.
intervention_text: If you noticed the wait was long but didn't flag it, think about what stopped you — was it unclear who to contact, or did you assume someone else was on it? Make the escalation automatic.

text: I always process outstanding balance payments as part of the check-out process.
description: Check-out is the right moment for financial conversations — a calm, dedicated exchange at reception is far more effective than anything that might happen in or near the surgery.
intervention_text: Outstanding balances that aren't addressed at check-out tend not to get addressed at all. If the conversation feels awkward, there's scripting in your learning resources to help.

text: I always answer phones within 3 rings, respond to texts within 3 minutes, and return emails within 3 hours.
description: Response time is often the first impression a prospective patient has of the practice — missing these targets means missed opportunities and signals that we're difficult to reach.
intervention_text: If you're consistently missing these SLAs, identify when it's happening most — first thing in the morning, during handovers, at lunch — find the pattern and fix the gap.

text: I always respond to new Boxly enquiries with a personal phone call within 10 minutes.
description: Enquiry leads go cold fast — a personal call within 10 minutes is one of the highest-converting actions available to a receptionist.
intervention_text: Every Boxly enquiry that waits longer than 10 minutes is a patient who has likely moved on. If the timing is genuinely difficult, flag it — this SLA may need a process change to protect.

text: I always place a caller on brief hold at the first natural break when a patient walks in, so I can serve the person in front of me.
description: The patient in front of you deserves undivided attention — managing this gracefully also signals to callers that we're thorough, not dismissive.
intervention_text: Trying to handle both at once usually means doing neither well. If this feels awkward, practise the hold script until it comes naturally before the next time it's needed.

text: I always check answering machine messages and missed calls in the morning, at lunch, and in the afternoon and take action as necessary.
description: Missed calls that don't get returned promptly are a direct source of lost new patients and frustrated existing ones.
intervention_text: If message checks have been slipping, set a phone or calendar reminder for each of the three check times until the habit is locked in.

text: I always fully complete the check-in process with an offer of hospitality before returning to other tasks.
description: A rushed check-in where the patient is directed to sit down without a warm close leaves them feeling processed rather than welcomed.
intervention_text: Think about what a complete check-in actually looks like — does the patient know what to expect next? Have they been offered a drink? If either is missing, the check-in isn't finished.

text: I always begin check-in by confirming the patient's preferred name and the identity of any accompanying person.
description: Getting a patient's name right from the first moment is a powerful signal of respect — and confirming accompanying persons is an important safeguarding habit.
intervention_text: This is one of those moves that can feel unnecessary until it matters — and when it matters, it really matters. Make it the first thing you do, every time.

text: I always confirm the patient's registration and medical history status prior to completing check-in.
description: Incomplete records are a compliance risk and slow down the clinical team — catching them at the front desk prevents delays that ripple through the entire appointment.
intervention_text: If records are frequently incomplete at check-in, the earlier touchpoints — booking and reminder communications — may need strengthening. Flag this to your manager.

text: I always set aside time each day to contact patients on the incomplete paperwork list.
description: Proactively chasing incomplete paperwork prevents check-in delays and keeps the clinical team's day running smoothly.
intervention_text: This is easy to defer when the day is busy, but it compounds quickly. Even 15 minutes a day, consistently applied, makes a significant difference to same-day stress. When can you protect this time?

text: I always personally contact any patient whose appointment remains unconfirmed 48 hours out.
description: Unconfirmed appointments are a leading predictor of no-shows — a personal contact at 48 hours gives enough time to fill the slot if the patient cancels.
intervention_text: If appointments are going unconfirmed past the 48-hour mark, check whether your end-of-day diary review is reliably catching these. Is there a process gap, or has the habit slipped?

text: I always use CareStack's list function to identify and contact patients for every empty surgery slot.
description: An empty surgery slot is lost revenue — the CareStack list function is the fastest tool available to fill it before it's gone.
intervention_text: If empty slots are going unfilled, review how regularly you're working the CareStack list. The contact list is only useful if it's being actioned every day.

text: I always ensure there are zero pending follow-up items in the VoiceStack Opportunities tab by the end of each day.
description: Every item left in Opportunities overnight is a potential patient who wasn't followed up — clearing the tab daily ensures nothing is missed.
intervention_text: Items in Opportunities tend to stack up quickly if they carry over. Make clearing the tab the last thing you do before signing off each day.

text: I always tidy the reception area and check the patient toilet and amenities at least once per hour.
description: The reception area is the physical expression of the practice's standards — a clean, stocked environment tells patients they're in a place that pays attention to detail.
intervention_text: If the hourly check has been slipping, set a recurring reminder or build it into natural breaks in the diary. Patients notice more than we tend to assume.

text: I always check throughout the day that the correct music is playing at an appropriate volume.
description: The practice's ambient environment is a subtle but real part of the patient experience, and it's entirely within reception's control.
intervention_text: This is a small thing that's easy to overlook when the day is busy — but it's part of owning the waiting area. A quick check takes seconds.

text: I always inform patients who cancel with less than 48 hours' notice of the consequence and offer one last opportunity to keep the appointment.
description: Enforcing the cancellation policy consistently — and with empathy — protects the diary and sends a clear message that appointments have real value.
intervention_text: If this conversation feels uncomfortable, remember the policy protects the patient's access to care as much as anything else. Scripting is available in your learning resources.

text: I always communicate the importance of attendance and ask the patient if we can count on them when booking.
description: A simple, direct question about commitment at the point of booking dramatically increases the psychological weight a patient places on their appointment.
intervention_text: This is easy to skip in the flow of a booking call, but it's one of the most effective no-show prevention tools available. Try adding it to your standard booking close.

text: I always inform patients of outstanding balances during appointment confirmation so they are prepared at check-in.
description: Patients who are surprised by a balance at check-in are more likely to dispute or delay payment — a heads-up during confirmation removes the surprise entirely.
intervention_text: If you're skipping this step during confirmation calls, the check-in experience is likely to be more awkward as a result. Make it a standard part of the confirmation script.

text: I always acknowledge patients who arrive late, express understanding, and advise that their wait may be longer than usual.
description: A late patient who receives a calm, empathetic response is far less likely to become a difficult one — and honest expectations prevent escalation.
intervention_text: The temptation when a late patient arrives is to say as little as possible. A brief, warm acknowledgement and an honest heads-up about wait time almost always defuses the tension.

text: I always remain calm and restate the patient's feedback when presented with a complaint or concern.
description: Restating the feedback signals to the patient that they've been genuinely heard — and it creates a moment to regulate your own response before reacting.
intervention_text: If a complaint caught you off guard and this didn't happen, think about what you'd say next time. Restating doesn't require agreeing — it just means reflecting back what you heard.

text: I always acknowledge my personal or our collective role in the situation when handling critical feedback.
description: Patients in complaint mode are not looking for excuses — they're looking to feel understood, and a genuine acknowledgement almost always de-escalates the conversation.
intervention_text: This isn't about blame — it's about signalling maturity and care. Even 'I can see why that was frustrating' is enough to shift the dynamic significantly.

text: I always ensure a clear next step or resolution is agreed before ending any interaction involving a complaint.
description: Complaints that end without a clear next step leave the patient dissatisfied and the team exposed — a named resolution closes the loop for everyone.
intervention_text: If the conversation ended without a clear next step, the patient is likely still frustrated. It's not too late to follow up with a call to offer one.

text: I always ask patients what their goals are for the visit and note the answer when booking.
description: Knowing why a patient has booked — beyond the appointment type — allows the whole team to personalise the experience and spot case acceptance opportunities.
intervention_text: This question feels unusual at first, but patients respond well to it — it signals that the practice is genuinely interested in them as a person. Try it on your next new patient booking call.

text: I always address the patient by their preferred name throughout every interaction.
description: Using a patient's preferred name — not just the name in the system — is one of the simplest ways to signal that they're a person, not an appointment slot.
intervention_text: If you're defaulting to whatever name is in CareStack without checking, make preferred name your first confirmation at every check-in.

text: I always ask at least one curious, open-ended question during check-in.
description: A single genuine question during check-in transforms a transactional interaction into a human one — and patients who feel noticed are more loyal and more likely to refer.
intervention_text: It doesn't have to be profound — 'How's your day going?' asked with real interest is enough. The goal is one moment of genuine connection per check-in. What stopped that from happening?

text: I always write a personalised response to every positive Google review within 24 hours.
description: A timely, personal response to a positive review reinforces the patient's good experience and signals to prospective patients that the practice is attentive and grateful.
intervention_text: If reviews are going without a response, it sends the signal that the practice doesn't really care — the opposite of the impression the review was building. Block 10 minutes a day to check.

text: I always call patients the day after their treatment to check in on their recovery and answer any questions.
description: A post-treatment call is a rare but high-impact gesture — most practices don't do it, and patients genuinely remember it.
intervention_text: If yesterday's treatment patients haven't been called, add them to your action list for first thing this morning. A 2-minute check-in can prevent a negative review and build real loyalty.

text: I always stand up and greet every patient with a smile.
description: Standing to greet a patient is an immediately disarming gesture — it signals that their arrival matters and sets the tone for everything that follows.
intervention_text: This is one of the simplest moves on the list and one of the most impactful. If it's not happening consistently, identify what's getting in the way — a call, a screen — and clear the space.

text: I always offer patients a hot or cold drink after check-in is complete.
description: An offer of hospitality communicates that the practice values the patient's time and comfort, not just their appointment slot.
intervention_text: If the offer is being skipped because check-in feels rushed, that's a signal to slow down — a complete check-in always includes the hospitality close.

text: I always dress in business casual attire at the practice, even on non-clinical days.
description: Consistent professional presentation maintains the practice's image and reinforces that reception is part of the clinical team, not separate from it.
intervention_text: Presentation is the first thing a patient registers — even before you speak. If this slipped, it's an easy reset for tomorrow.

text: I always centre myself and smile before answering the phone to ensure a warm tone of voice.
description: A patient calling the practice has no other signal of its quality except the voice they hear — the energy you bring to the phone is the practice's first impression.
intervention_text: If calls have been feeling rushed or flat lately, try physically pausing before picking up. One breath and a smile sounds small, but it genuinely changes the quality of what follows.

text: I always respond to cost concerns by presenting all available payment, financing, and membership plan options.
description: A patient who raises a cost concern hasn't said no — they've opened a door. Having all the options ready and presenting them confidently converts hesitation into treatment.
intervention_text: If cost conversations feel awkward, the options probably aren't fully internalised yet. Make sure you know the membership plan pricing, any payment schedule options, and the treatment discount by heart.

text: I always preview the dentist by name and reference a specific detail about their expertise when booking a new patient appointment.
description: A patient who knows something specific about their dentist before they arrive is already more trusting — credibility building starts on the booking call, not in the surgery.
intervention_text: If you're not sure what to say about a particular dentist, ask them directly: 'What should I tell patients about you?' Make a note — you only need to do this once per dentist.

text: I always describe the modern technologies, materials, and clinical processes used at our practice when booking a new patient appointment.
description: Proactively mentioning the practice's technology during a new patient call signals quality, justifies premium fees, and starts differentiating from NHS alternatives before the patient even arrives.
intervention_text: If the tech conversation feels forced, it's usually because it's being treated as an add-on rather than part of the natural new patient script. Work it in at a consistent point in the call.

text: I always guide new patients through completing their patient portal registration during the booking call.
description: Patients who complete their portal registration before they arrive experience a smoother, faster check-in — and it prevents the frustration of delays on the day.
intervention_text: If patients are frequently arriving with incomplete registration, the booking call is where to fix it. Stay on the line with them — even if it takes a few extra minutes, it saves more time than it costs.

text: I always verbally preview all aspects of a visit when booking a new patient appointment.
description: A patient who knows exactly what to expect — scan, nurse introduction, consultation structure — arrives calmer and requires less reassurance at the chair.
intervention_text: If patients frequently arrive with questions about what's going to happen, the preview on the booking call probably isn't complete. Walk through every stage of the visit and make sure each one gets a sentence.

text: I always follow our clinical question triage process when a patient raises a query outside my knowledge.
description: Clinical questions that reach the wrong person — or no person — erode patient trust and create risk. The triage process exists to make sure every question gets the right answer quickly.
intervention_text: If this process felt unclear or inconsistent, the triage guide is in your learning resources. Knowing exactly who to contact and in what order removes the hesitation that causes delays.

text: I always confirm that all required consent forms have been completed via the patient portal at least one week before any treatment appointment.
description: Consent forms completed in advance give patients time to read and raise questions, reduce chair-side admin, and protect the practice from compliance risk.
intervention_text: If consent forms are regularly incomplete at the time of treatment, the one-week follow-up step is likely being missed. Set a calendar trigger for each upcoming treatment appointment to check and chase.

text: I always introduce our membership plan during every new patient enquiry call.
description: The first enquiry call is the highest-leverage moment to introduce the plan — the patient is engaged, forming their first impression, and most open to understanding the practice's full offer.
intervention_text: If the plan isn't coming up on enquiry calls, it's probably because it feels like a sales pitch at the wrong moment. It isn't — it's information that makes the practice more attractive. Work it into your enquiry script.

text: I always present our membership plan to non-members at the end of every new patient appointment.
description: A patient who has just experienced the practice for the first time is at peak willingness to commit — this is the moment to present the plan and convert.
intervention_text: If the plan presentation is being skipped at the end of new patient appointments, it's a direct loss to practice revenue. Check CareStack to confirm membership status before the patient arrives at check-out.

text: I always check a patient's membership plan status in CareStack before every appointment and reference the plan with non-members at check-out.
description: Consistently surfacing the plan at every appointment — not just new patient ones — is what prevents long-term patients from remaining non-members indefinitely.
intervention_text: If membership status isn't part of your pre-appointment preparation, it's easy to miss. Add it to your check-in checklist so it becomes automatic.

text: I always ask the dentist to review my clinical notes for accuracy before they leave the chair.
description: A quick confirmation from the dentist before they move on is the simplest quality control step in the room — it catches errors when they're easiest to fix.
intervention_text: If the dentist left without reviewing the notes, any errors in the record now require a separate correction. Make the review request a standard close to every charting session — it takes seconds.

text: I always accurately record the correct conditions for the correct teeth in both the clinical notes and on the dental chart as the dentist calls out findings.
description: Charting errors are among the most consequential mistakes in clinical dentistry — an accurate, real-time record depends entirely on focused, precise notation as findings are called out.
intervention_text: If errors were made during charting, identify where the breakdown happened — was it the speed, the terminology, or a distraction? Accuracy in the moment is always easier than correcting the record after the fact.

text: I always accurately record all mutually agreed treatment as the dentist presents options to the patient.
description: Treatment that is agreed in the chair but not captured accurately in the record creates confusion at every subsequent appointment — precise real-time recording is part of the clinical standard, not an admin task.
intervention_text: If the agreed treatment wasn't fully recorded, the next clinical encounter is starting with an incomplete picture. Review what was agreed and update the notes before the patient's next appointment.

text: I always collect new patients from reception, conduct their intraoral scan, and prepare the scan report before introducing them to their dentist.
description: The new patient intake sequence — scan first, then introduction to the dentist — means the dentist walks in with a complete diagnostic picture, and the patient has already experienced the practice's technology before treatment is discussed.
intervention_text: If the scan wasn't completed before the dentist arrived, the appointment lost one of its key quality signals. Protect the sequence: reception handoff → scan → report → dentist introduction, every time.

text: I always anticipate the next instrument the dentist will need and have it ready before they ask for it.
description: A nurse who anticipates rather than reacts keeps the surgeon in flow and reduces the cognitive load in the room — this is one of the most visible markers of clinical competence.
intervention_text: If you were caught without the right instrument and the dentist had to ask, think about where the procedure was heading at that moment. Anticipation improves with procedure familiarity — identify which procedures still feel unpredictable and focus there.

competency_name: Patient Comfort and Communication During Procedures
text: I always tell, show, and do before performing any action on a patient.
description: Tell-show-do is one of the most effective anxiety management tools in clinical dentistry — patients who know what's coming are measurably calmer and more cooperative than those who don't.
intervention_text: If a patient flinched, tensed, or asked what you were doing mid-procedure, the tell-show-do step was likely missed. Build it in as a non-negotiable before every clinical action, even routine ones.

competency_name: Patient Comfort and Communication During Procedures
text: I always notice and verbally affirm specific positive behaviours from the patient during clinical activities.
description: Specific, genuine reinforcement — 'you're doing brilliantly at staying still' — is far more effective than generic praise and meaningfully reduces patient anxiety across the appointment.
intervention_text: Generic reassurance like 'you're doing great' lands less than specific feedback. Think about what the patient actually did well and name it — the more specific it is, the more it lands.

competency_name: Patient Comfort and Communication During Procedures
text: I always monitor the patient for signs of anxiety or discomfort during procedures and actively manage their comfort unless the dentist is already doing so.
description: An unmanaged anxious patient affects the quality of the procedure and their likelihood of returning — proactive comfort monitoring is part of the clinical role, not a nice-to-have.
intervention_text: If a patient was visibly tense and it wasn't addressed, think about what you were focused on instead. Comfort monitoring is a parallel task, not a separate one — it happens at the same time as everything else.

competency_name: Patient Comfort and Communication During Procedures
text: When the dentist enters, I always present the patient by name, state the planned procedure, share any relevant medical history, and relay any patient questions or concerns.
description: A thorough patient presentation means the dentist walks in fully informed and the patient feels seen — it sets the clinical standard for the appointment from the first moment.
intervention_text: If the dentist had to ask for information during the appointment that should have been in the presentation, the handoff was incomplete. Standardise what you include every time: name, procedure, medical history, patient concerns.

competency_name: Patient Comfort and Communication During Procedures
text: I always ask patients what they'd like to watch or listen to during their appointment and make sure they can see and hear it clearly before treatment begins.
description: A patient who is comfortably settled with their chosen entertainment is measurably more relaxed and easier to treat — getting this right before treatment starts prevents interruptions mid-procedure.
intervention_text: If this was skipped or the setup wasn't quite right, the patient may have been uncomfortable in ways that were avoidable. Make the entertainment setup part of your patient-seating routine — it takes less than a minute.

competency_name: Patient Comfort and Communication During Procedures
text: I always preview the dentist and the procedure before treatment begins and invite any questions or concerns from the patient.
description: A brief preview before treatment starts gives the patient a final moment to ask questions and mentally prepare — it reduces mid-procedure interruptions and builds trust in the care they're about to receive.
intervention_text: If the procedure started without a preview, the patient may have felt rushed or uncertain. Build the preview into your patient setup close — after the entertainment is sorted and before you call the dentist in.

text: I always use gloves only when handling contaminated instruments or chemicals and remove them before touching anything clean or sterile.
description: Glove discipline is one of the foundational infection control behaviours — incorrect use is a direct cross-contamination risk and a compliance issue that inspectors look for specifically.
intervention_text: If glove use was inconsistent during this session, identify the moment it slipped and why. This is a non-negotiable standard — the consequence of getting it wrong is clinical, not just procedural.

text: I always set up the tray for the scheduled procedure and any likely alternatives before bringing the patient into the surgery.
description: A fully prepared tray before the patient enters removes the need to leave the room mid-procedure and signals a level of preparation that patients notice and trust.
intervention_text: If the tray wasn't ready when the patient arrived, it created a delay and a gap in the professional impression. Review the appointment list at the start of each session so setups are never reactive.

text: I always review the surgery reset checklist and confirm every item is complete before considering the surgery ready for the next patient.
description: A missed reset item — contaminated surface, incorrectly stored instrument, incomplete stock — is an infection control risk that compounds across every appointment that follows.
intervention_text: If the reset was rushed or the checklist wasn't completed in full, the surgery may not have been truly ready. The checklist exists because memory alone isn't reliable at the end of a busy session.

text: I always use fresh cleaning cloths for each individual patient appointment.
description: Reusing cleaning cloths between patients is a cross-contamination risk — even if surfaces appear clean, the clinical standard requires a fresh cloth for every appointment without exception.
intervention_text: This is a non-negotiable infection control standard. If it slipped, identify what pressured the shortcut — time, supply, habit — and address it before the next session.

text: I always verify that valid consent has been obtained before starting the appointment.
description: Consent is a non-negotiable legal and ethical requirement — checking it before every appointment, not just assuming it's been done, protects both the patient and the practice.
intervention_text: If an appointment started without confirmed consent, that's a compliance risk regardless of outcome. Make the consent check the first thing you do when reviewing the patient record, every time.

text: I always label the teeth on the images after taking a radiograph before leaving the workstation.
description: Unlabelled radiographs create ambiguity in clinical records and slow down the dentist's review — correct labelling at the workstation before you move prevents errors that are difficult to fix retrospectively.
intervention_text: If images left the workstation unlabelled, the clinical record is incomplete. Build the labelling step into your radiograph routine before you do anything else after the exposure.

text: I always update the patient status to "In Chair" when they are seated and "Treatment Complete" when they are ready for reception.
description: Accurate, real-time status updates are what allow reception and the wider team to manage the diary without constantly checking in — a delayed update creates a ripple that affects everyone.
intervention_text: If status updates are being delayed or forgotten, reception is flying blind. Make the update the first thing you do when a patient sits down and the last thing before you walk them to the lounge.

text: I always consult the lead dental nurse and create a plan to get back on time when the patient time tracker shows a warning.
description: Running late in one surgery affects the whole day's flow — catching a warning early and acting on it is far less disruptive than letting a delay compound across every appointment that follows.
intervention_text: If the warning was noticed but nothing was done, the delay was avoidable. The point of the tracker is to prompt action, not just awareness — what would getting back on time have required?

text: I always communicate patient readiness to the dentist clearly, including the patient's location, procedure, and type, so the surgery keeps moving.
description: The dentist can only flow efficiently between patients if the information they receive is complete and consistent — vague or incomplete handovers create hesitation and lost time.
intervention_text: If the dentist had to ask for information that should have been communicated, that's a flow breakdown. Standardise what you say when a patient is ready and make it a reflex.

text: I always maintain the same professional pace and focus whether the surgery is calm or hectic.
description: Patients and dentists both read the nurse's energy — a nurse who appears rushed or flustered in a busy session raises anxiety in the room. Consistency under pressure is a skill, not just an attitude.
intervention_text: If your pace or manner shifted noticeably under pressure, think about what triggered it. Identifying the pattern is the first step to managing it before it affects the patient or the session.

text: I always check Dentistry Compliance and complete all outstanding tasks before leaving the practice each day.
description: End-of-day compliance tasks exist to keep the practice safe, legal, and operationally sound — tasks that carry over accumulate risk and create extra work for the following day.
intervention_text: If tasks were left incomplete, the practice started the next day with a backlog and a compliance gap. Build a Dentistry Compliance check into your end-of-day routine before you start tidying up.

text: I always check in with reception during any gap of 45 minutes or more, once my nursing duties are complete, to offer help contacting patients on the short-notice list.
description: A nurse who can use downtime productively is a genuine asset to the whole practice — filling a gap in the diary benefits everyone, and the offer costs nothing if reception already has it covered.
intervention_text: If downtime passed without a check-in with reception, a slot may have gone unfilled that didn't have to. The habit is simple: nursing duties first, then check in — it only takes a moment.

text: I always check high-turnover disposables before lunch and at the end of the day and flag anything running low.
description: Running short on disposables mid-session creates unnecessary stress and can disrupt patient care — two checks a day is all it takes to make sure it never happens.
intervention_text: If a session started short on supplies, the pre-session check was missed. It takes less than two minutes and prevents a problem that's much harder to fix once a patient is in the chair.

text: I always book the patient's 6-month recall appointment before they leave the surgery.
description: Booking recalls in the chair — before the patient reaches reception — removes a point of friction, captures the appointment while the patient is engaged, and takes one task off reception's plate.
intervention_text: If the patient left without a recall booked, there's now a gap in the diary that requires a follow-up call to fill. Build the recall booking into your end-of-appointment routine before you walk the patient to the lounge.

text: I always mention our membership plan to new patients at the end of their appointment and let them know a receptionist will tell them more on their way out.
description: A warm introduction to the plan from the nurse — before the patient reaches reception — means reception is inheriting a patient who's already curious, not hearing about it for the first time.
intervention_text: If the plan wasn't mentioned, reception is starting the conversation cold. A single sentence at the end of the appointment is all it takes to set the handoff up well.

text: I always check the patient's clinical notes and confirm a complete medical history before beginning the appointment.
description: Starting an appointment without reviewing the notes is a clinical risk — allergies, contraindications, and relevant history need to be confirmed before any treatment begins, not discovered mid-procedure.
intervention_text: If this check was skipped, the appointment began with incomplete information. Make the notes review non-negotiable, even for regular patients — medical histories change.

text: I always take at least one intraoral photograph after each applicable procedure to support patient understanding and clinical records.
description: Intraoral photos serve a dual purpose — they strengthen the clinical record and give patients a visual anchor when discussing their treatment, which directly supports case acceptance.
intervention_text: If photos weren't taken, both the record and the case acceptance opportunity are weaker than they should be. Build the photo step into your post-procedure routine before you update the notes.

text: I always complete and save clinical notes as a draft before the end of each appointment.
description: Notes that aren't saved before the patient leaves rely on memory — the accuracy of clinical records degrades quickly once the next patient is in the chair.
intervention_text: If notes were left incomplete or unsaved, the clinical record is at risk. Draft notes before the patient is walked to the lounge — it doesn't need to be final, but it needs to be saved.

text: I always take a moment to assess the patient's mood once they are in the chair and quietly flag any concerns to the dentist.
description: Mood assessment before treatment begins allows the clinical team to adapt their approach — a dentist who knows a patient is anxious or distressed can adjust before the appointment becomes difficult.
intervention_text: If a patient's emotional state went unread and it affected the appointment, think about what signals were there. Building a brief, deliberate moment of assessment into your chair routine makes this a habit rather than a reaction.

text: I always tell the patient before beginning any clinical activity that they can raise their hand at any time to ask me to pause.
description: Giving the patient an explicit signal of control is one of the most effective anxiety reduction tools in the surgery — it costs nothing and meaningfully changes how safe a patient feels.
intervention_text: If this wasn't said before treatment began, the patient had no clear way to ask for a pause without feeling disruptive. Make it the first thing you say before you pick anything up.

text: I always pause for one deep breath to centre myself before speaking or acting when I notice my own stress rising.
description: A nurse who manages their own stress visibly in the room keeps the energy calm — patients are highly attuned to clinical staff anxiety, and it transfers directly to them.
intervention_text: If you noticed your own stress affecting your manner or pace, that's the signal this move is for. One breath is not a delay — it's a reset that costs nothing and changes everything that follows.

text: I always emphasise the importance of the next appointment and explain the consequences of missing it once it is booked.
description: A patient who understands why the next appointment matters is significantly more likely to keep it — this conversation takes 20 seconds and meaningfully reduces no-shows.
intervention_text: If the next appointment was booked without this conversation, the patient may not place the right weight on it. Add it to your recall booking close — it works best as a direct, caring statement, not a warning.

text: I always invite patients to leave a Google review or record a short video testimonial during their lounge wait.
description: The lounge wait is the highest-value moment to ask for a review — the patient's experience is fresh, they're settled, and they have time. A direct, warm invitation converts far more often than a passive QR code.
intervention_text: If the invitation wasn't made, a review opportunity was missed. The ask doesn't need to be long — 'While you wait, would you mind leaving us a quick Google review? It really helps the practice.' is enough.

text: I always remain calm and restate the patient's feedback as my first response to any complaint or concern.
description: Restating what a patient said signals that they've been genuinely heard — and it gives you a moment to regulate before reacting, which almost always improves what happens next.
intervention_text: If you responded before restating, the patient may have felt cut off or defensive. The restate is a one-sentence pause — it doesn't require agreement, just reflection of what you heard.

text: I always follow a restatement with "tell me more" and actively listen to the response.
description: "Tell me more" is one of the most disarming phrases in a feedback conversation — it signals genuine curiosity, slows the interaction down, and almost always reveals the real issue beneath the surface complaint.
intervention_text: If the conversation escalated after the restate, the 'tell me more' step was likely missed. It's a small pivot that shifts the dynamic from defensive to collaborative — practise making it automatic.

text: I always ensure a clear next step or resolution is agreed before ending any interaction involving a complaint or conflict.
description: A complaint that ends without a named resolution leaves the patient dissatisfied and the team exposed — closing with a clear next step signals professionalism and prevents the issue from resurfacing.
intervention_text: If the interaction ended without a clear resolution, the patient is probably still frustrated. It's not too late to follow up — a brief check-in after the appointment can close the loop effectively.

text: I always greet the patient by name, make eye contact, and introduce myself by name.
description: A personal, direct greeting from the first team member the patient encounters in the clinical area sets the tone for everything that follows — it signals that they're a person, not a procedure.
intervention_text: If the greeting was rushed or generic, the patient's first clinical impression was a missed opportunity. Practise making name, eye contact, and self-introduction simultaneous and natural.

text: I always ask the patient a curious, open-ended question as I am seating them in the chair.
description: A single genuine question while seating the patient transforms the start of an appointment from transactional to human — patients who feel noticed are calmer, more engaged, and more loyal.
intervention_text: This is easy to skip when you're focused on setup. The question doesn't have to be profound — 'How's your day been?' with genuine interest is enough. What stopped it from happening?

text: I always offer patients a blanket or a drink before any procedure.
description: A genuine offer of comfort before treatment begins communicates that the patient's experience matters as much as the clinical outcome — it's a small gesture with a disproportionate impact on how safe patients feel.
intervention_text: If the offer was skipped because things felt rushed, that's the signal to slow down for 30 seconds. The offer is part of the patient setup, not an optional extra.

text: I always ask the patient "How does that sound to you?" or "How are you feeling about this plan?" after reiterating a treatment plan.
description: An open question after the plan recap gives the patient permission to voice any doubt before they leave the chair — catching hesitation here is far easier than recovering it at the front desk.
intervention_text: If this didn't happen, the patient may have walked out unclear or uncertain about their treatment. Practise making this question automatic — it takes three seconds and changes the outcome of the whole appointment.

text: I always check for the patient's comprehension and clearly narrate the next steps once the dentist has explained the treatment and left the chair.
description: The moment the dentist leaves is when confusion sets in for most patients — a clear, calm narration of what happens next gives them something concrete to hold onto.
intervention_text: Patients who leave without a clear picture of next steps are more likely to disengage or not follow through. Think about whether you gave a full narration, or just assumed the dentist's explanation was enough.

text: I always invite the patient to share back the key parts of the post-operative plan to confirm their understanding and comfort with next steps.
description: Asking a patient to summarise what they've heard is the most reliable way to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a problem — it also signals that you genuinely care about their experience after they leave.
intervention_text: If you skipped this, there's a real chance the patient is going home with incomplete or incorrect information. Make the teach-back a non-negotiable close to every post-treatment conversation.

text: I always reassure a patient who is uncertain about a procedure, acknowledge its importance, and let the dentist know about the conversation.
description: A patient who expresses uncertainty is giving you an opportunity — addressed calmly and honestly in the chair, it's far more likely to convert than if it surfaces later at the front desk.
intervention_text: If a patient's uncertainty wasn't addressed, it's likely they'll either cancel or decline treatment down the line. Even a brief reassurance and a note to the dentist can shift that outcome.

text: I always verbally link the dentist's recommended treatment to the patient's desired outcome.
description: Patients accept treatment when they understand what it does for them specifically — connecting the recommendation to their own goals makes the value personal and concrete.
intervention_text: Generic explanations of treatment tend not to land. Think about whether you connected the recommendation to something the patient actually said they wanted — if not, try it next time.

text: I always identify whether a patient's hesitation is about comfort, time, or cost before responding to it.
description: Responding to the wrong concern wastes time and can make a patient feel unheard — pinpointing the real issue first means your response actually addresses what's holding them back.
intervention_text: If the hesitation wasn't resolved, it may be because the response didn't match the actual concern. Ask one clarifying question before jumping to reassurance.

text: I always reassure patients with cost concerns that treatment can be staged safely, and I pass their concerns to reception.
description: Staging reassurance keeps patients in the treatment journey rather than walking away — and handing the cost conversation to reception ensures it's handled in the right environment with the right options.
intervention_text: If a patient left with unresolved cost concerns and reception wasn't informed, there's a high chance that treatment won't proceed. Build the handoff to reception into how you close cost conversations in the chair.

text: I always highlight the health risks of delaying treatment or dental check-ups when confirming next steps with the patient.
description: Patients who understand the consequence of waiting are more motivated to follow through — this isn't fear-mongering, it's giving them the information they need to make a genuinely informed choice.
intervention_text: If next steps were confirmed without mentioning the risk of delay, the patient may not place enough urgency on following through. A single sentence about what changes if they wait can make a real difference.

text: After the appointment, I always walk the patient to the lounge, offer hospitality, and let them know a receptionist will be with them shortly to go through their next steps.
description: The post-appointment transition is a key moment in the patient experience — a warm, unhurried handoff from nurse to lounge sets the patient up for a positive financial conversation and reinforces that the practice values their time.
intervention_text: If the patient was directed to reception without a warm handoff, the financial conversation may have started on the back foot. The lounge transition is part of your role — it's not complete until the patient is settled and knows what to expect next.

text: I always introduce the patient to their dentist by name and comment specifically on their expertise or experience.
description: A personal, specific introduction to the dentist builds instant credibility and trust — it signals that this is a team that knows each other well, not a conveyor belt of strangers.
intervention_text: A generic or skipped introduction is a missed opportunity to set the patient's confidence before treatment even begins. Ask each dentist what they'd like patients to know about them so you always have something specific to say.

text: I always highlight our advanced diagnostic technology — including 3D intraoral scanning, our on-site CBCT scanner, and AI-assisted imaging — when setting up the patient before the dentist arrives.
description: Patients who understand what our technology does and why it matters are more confident in their diagnosis and more receptive to recommended treatment — credibility building happens well before the dentist walks in.
intervention_text: If the tech wasn't mentioned, the patient experienced a high-quality diagnostic process without understanding its value. Build a brief tech mention into your patient setup routine so it becomes natural.

text: I always share a brief, positive story about how a similar treatment helped a patient, without using any names or identifying details.
description: Social proof in the chair is powerful — a real, brief story makes the benefit of treatment tangible and personal in a way that clinical explanation alone rarely does.
intervention_text: If you're not using stories, treatments can feel abstract to patients. Keep one or two genuine examples in mind for the most common procedures — they don't need to be dramatic to be effective.

text: I always schedule time each week to observe the dental nurse to dentist hand-over, document at least one opportunity for improvement, and follow up with the appropriate team member about it.
description: The nurse-to-dentist hand-over is one of the highest-leverage clinical touchpoints in the practice — a manager who observes and documents it weekly creates a continuous improvement loop that no amount of training alone can replicate.
intervention_text: If this wasn't observed this week, think about what got in the way. Protecting this time in the diary rather than fitting it around everything else is the only way to make it reliable.

text: I always review all equipment maintenance tasks in Dentistry Compliance with my Lead Nurse each week and ensure every item is either completed or has a clear due date before the end of that week.
description: Equipment maintenance tasks that carry over without a clear resolution date create compounding compliance risk — weekly review with the Lead Nurse keeps accountability joint and prevents anything from quietly slipping.
intervention_text: If items carried over without a clear due date, the compliance record has a gap. Review what's outstanding now and assign a named date and owner to every open item before the end of today.

text: I always maintain an up-to-date evidence file for each of the CQC's five key questions so the practice can demonstrate compliance at any point, not only ahead of a scheduled inspection.
description: The CQC can inspect unannounced and inspects against five key questions: Safe, Effective, Caring, Responsive, and Well-led. A manager who builds evidence continuously is never caught out — one who only prepares when an inspection is expected is taking a serious reputational and regulatory risk.
intervention_text: If the evidence file hasn't been updated recently, the practice is not currently inspection-ready. Block time this week to review each of the five key questions and identify where the evidence is thin or out of date.

text: I always review the previous week's key KPIs every Monday — including gross production, new patient numbers, membership growth, and Google reviews — identify any problem areas, and present a clear action plan to the practice principal.
description: Weekly KPI review is how a manager stays ahead of problems rather than reacting to them — and presenting a named action plan to the principal signals ownership rather than just reporting.
intervention_text: If Monday's review didn't happen or produced no action plan, the week is already starting without a clear direction. Even a 20-minute review with one or two named actions is significantly better than none.

text: I always verify that the team is meeting our patient communication standards — response times, message handling, and enquiry follow-up — and address any consistent gaps directly with the relevant team member.
description: The manager's job is to hold the standard, not execute the tasks. A receptionist who knows their manager is actively monitoring response times and message handling performs to a higher standard than one who doesn't.
intervention_text: If communication standards slipped this week and it wasn't addressed, the team has received an implicit signal that the standard is flexible. Identify the specific gap, name it directly with the team member, and confirm it's been resolved.

text: I always verify that appointment confirmations and outstanding patient paperwork are being actioned to the required standard and give clear direction to the team when they are not.
description: Confirmation and paperwork gaps are two of the most predictable sources of no-shows and check-in delays — a manager who monitors these proactively protects the diary and the clinical team's day.
intervention_text: If confirmations or paperwork tasks were missed this week without being addressed, review what the current gap looks like in CareStack and agree a clear catch-up plan with the reception team today.

text: I always review NPS scores at the end of each week, note any outliers, and plan a specific response — either a celebration or an investigation — for the following week.
description: NPS outliers — positive or negative — always contain signal. A manager who reads them weekly and acts on them consistently turns patient feedback into a genuine improvement system rather than a vanity metric.
intervention_text: If this week's NPS review didn't happen, there may be feedback sitting unread that warrants a response. Even a quick scan for anything outside the normal range takes less than 10 minutes and keeps you ahead of patterns before they become trends.

text: I always review case acceptance rates weekly with the TCO, identify any patterns in unconverted cases, and agree specific actions to address gaps.
description: Case acceptance rate is one of the clearest indicators of where the patient journey is breaking down — whether that's in the fee conversation, the plan presentation, or the follow-up process. The manager owns this review; the TCO owns the execution.
intervention_text: If this review didn't happen this week, the TCO is operating without oversight and unconverted cases may be stacking up without a clear recovery plan. Schedule the review before the end of the week and start with the oldest outstanding cases first.

text: I always verify that patients with outstanding balances have been contacted ahead of their appointment and follow up directly with the team if this step has been missed.
description: Outstanding balances that aren't flagged before an appointment create awkward, reactive conversations at check-in — a manager who monitors this proactively protects both the patient experience and the practice's cash position.
intervention_text: If patients arrived with unaddressed balances this week, trace back to where the follow-up was missed and confirm the process is clear for the team. The issue is rarely unwillingness — it's usually a lack of a clear, owned step in the workflow.

text: I always complete and submit the Daily Production Report and verify it matches the figures in CareStack before 10am the following day.
description: Daily production reporting is the financial heartbeat of the practice — a report that's late or unreconciled means decisions are being made on incomplete or inaccurate information.
intervention_text: If the report was late or unreconciled, identify what caused the delay and whether it's a recurring pattern. A one-off is manageable; a pattern signals that the process needs protecting in the day's structure.

text: I always review membership plan direct debits once a month and personally follow up on any failed debits.
description: Failed direct debits are quiet revenue leaks — they rarely resolve themselves, and patients are usually more receptive to a prompt, personal follow-up than a delayed one.
intervention_text: If failed debits from last month haven't been followed up, pull the report now. Each unresolved failed debit is both a revenue gap and a patient at risk of lapsing from the plan.

text: I always verify team attendance for both ProMove check-ins each week and follow up with any team member who misses one within one business day.
description: Consistent check-in attendance is the foundation of the ProMoves system — a manager who monitors and follows up on absences signals that development is non-negotiable, not optional.
intervention_text: If a team member missed a check-in this week and wasn't followed up with, they've received an implicit message that it doesn't really matter. A same-day or next-day follow-up is all it takes to reset that expectation.

text: I always walk the floor twice daily to check in briefly with every team member, address any immediate barriers, and give specific encouragement when I see something done well.
description: A manager who is physically present and specifically encouraging creates a fundamentally different team culture from one who manages primarily from an office — twice-daily floor walks are how great managers stay connected to the real state of the practice.
intervention_text: If the floor walks haven't been happening consistently, think about what's pulling you away from them. Managing by exception — only appearing when something's wrong — erodes team confidence faster than most managers realise.

text: I always model the patient experience standard with at least one patient each day so the team has a visible, live benchmark to work to.
description: A manager who does the job alongside the team — not just talks about the standard — is the most powerful form of coaching available. One visible, excellent check-in per day is worth more than a dozen briefings.
intervention_text: If this hasn't been happening, the team's standard is being set by whoever is most confident on the floor, not by you. Find one moment today to do a check-in at the standard you'd want to see and make sure the team can see it.

text: I always personally follow up with any patient concern or complaint escalated to me before the end of the following day, clearly summarising what we will do next and how they can reach me directly.
description: A manager who personally follows up on escalated complaints turns a negative experience into a trust-building one — the personal touch at the right moment is often the difference between a patient who leaves and one who becomes loyal.
intervention_text: If an escalated complaint wasn't followed up within 24 hours, contact the patient today. The longer the gap, the harder the recovery. A brief, direct call that names a clear next step is almost always enough to reset the relationship.

text: I always monitor the mood of the practice throughout the day and intervene as necessary — either resetting the tone with the team or addressing the source of tension directly with the individual involved.
description: Team energy is contagious in both directions — a manager who reads and actively manages the emotional atmosphere of the practice prevents small tensions from becoming disruptive ones and keeps the patient-facing team at their best.
intervention_text: If tension in the practice went unaddressed today, think about what you noticed and didn't act on. Even a quiet, private check-in with the relevant person is usually enough to prevent a small issue from becoming a bigger one.

text: I always ensure the staff schedule is published at least two weeks in advance and that any gaps from leave or sickness are covered before they affect a clinical day.
description: A schedule published with adequate notice allows the clinical team to plan and reduces last-minute coverage stress — gaps that aren't caught before the clinical day create a reactive, pressured environment that affects everyone's performance.
intervention_text: If the schedule isn't published two weeks out or has unresolved gaps, review it today. Each gap that reaches the clinical day without a resolution is a management failure that the whole team absorbs.

text: I always address performance concerns directly and promptly with the relevant team member in a private setting, and document the conversation and agreed next steps.
description: Performance concerns that aren't named directly tend to worsen — they also create an unfair environment for the team members who are performing well. A prompt, private conversation with a clear record is the professional standard.
intervention_text: If a performance concern is sitting unaddressed, think about what's making it difficult to raise. Delaying rarely makes the conversation easier — it usually makes it harder and the behaviour more entrenched.

text: I always hold a one-to-one conversation with each self-employed associate at least once a month to discuss their schedule, any clinical concerns, and their experience at the practice.
description: Self-employed associates require a different management approach — they can't be managed in the same way as employed staff, but they still need a regular, structured touchpoint to feel invested in and to raise concerns before they become reasons to leave.
intervention_text: If one-to-ones with associates have lapsed, the risk is that small frustrations are building without a channel to surface them. A brief, informal monthly conversation costs very little and significantly reduces the risk of a sudden disengagement.

text: I always confirm that the practice's social media content for the week has been gathered from the team and submitted to the marketing contact by the end of the last clinical day of the week.
description: Consistent social media presence requires consistent content — a manager who owns the weekly submission habit is the difference between a practice that appears active and credible online and one that posts sporadically.
intervention_text: If content wasn't submitted this week, the marketing contact is working without material and the practice's online presence has a gap. Make the submission the last task of the clinical week rather than something that gets pushed to Monday.

text: I always confirm that all pre-treatment admin — including consent forms, booked appointments, and any required patient communications — is completed at least one week before the scheduled treatment date.
description: Pre-treatment admin that isn't completed in advance creates rushed, stressful conversations at the chair-side and exposes the practice to consent and compliance risk. A one-week lead time creates enough space to catch and resolve anything that's missing.
intervention_text: If treatment is scheduled within the next week and pre-treatment admin is incomplete, escalate today. A week is tight but workable — anything less creates genuine clinical and compliance risk that isn't manageable at short notice.

text: I always ensure the TCO and front desk team are consistently presenting all available financial options — membership plan, staged treatment, and third-party finance — to patients with cost concerns.
description: Financial objections are rarely final — they're usually a request for help finding a way. A manager who monitors whether the team is consistently presenting all options ensures that no patient leaves without having heard a solution that might work for them.
intervention_text: If cost concerns are resulting in declined treatment without all options being presented, this is a training and accountability issue rather than a patient issue. Review with the TCO what's being said in these conversations and identify where the gap is.

competency_name: Patient Comfort and Communication During Procedures
text: I always observe each of my staff members during procedures once a month, and deliver positive and constructive feedback as appropriate.
I always verbally dictate to RDA/AI a clear and accurate baseline oral health status at new patient exams- current teeth present, existing treatment, and any findings present.
description: At new patient exams, I verbally call out existing restorations, missing teeth, and prior treatment so the RDA and AI can accurately document the patient’s starting dentition. Establishing a clear baseline ensures diagnostic accuracy, protects the practice from confusion or liability later, and creates a reliable record for future care.

text: I always update the odontogram and any clinical findings by verbally dictating them to the RDA/AI at each patient encounter.
description: At every exam, I verbally call out erupted, exfoliated, restored, or missing teeth so the RDA and AI can update the odontogram in real time. Keeping the odontogram current ensures the chart accurately reflects the patient’s dentition, improving diagnostic clarity, treatment planning, and continuity of care.

text: I always verbalize to the RDA/AI to chart any incipient lesions so that preventative care can be offered or teeth can be appropriately monitored radiographically.
description: During exams, I verbally identify incipient enamel lesions so the RDA and AI can accurately document them in the chart. Clearly charting early caries supports preventive treatment, improves monitoring over time, and ensures early disease is not overlooked or minimized.

text: I always explain cavities clearly- indicating to the parent there is a cavity in the first, second or third layer of tooth- instead of saying there is a "spot" "watch" or other minimizing language.
description: Minimizing language can lead to misunderstanding, delayed care, and erosion of trust. Clear language supports informed decision-making.

text: I always offer sealants on healthy posterior primary and permanent teeth, regardless of insurance coverage.
description: Sealants significantly reduce caries risk. Families deserve to know preventive options even if insurance does not cover them.

text: I always offer SDF (primary teeth) or Curodont (Permanent teeth) for incipient lesions.
description: Minimally invasive options allow early intervention and avoid progression.

text: I always ensure bitewings and any necessary PA's are taken every 6 months for patients with incipient lesions, history of caries or treatment in last 2 years, history of dental trauma, pulp therapy or other indications that would make them high caries risk or require more frequent follow up.
description: Higher-risk patients require more frequent and targeted imaging to avoid missed disease.

text: I always instruct RDAs to take PAs for any teeth planned for extraction or pulp therapy, or with caries approaching the pulp.
description: PAs are essential for accurate diagnosis and informed consent prior to more invasive treatment.

text: I always perform a comprehensive evaluation and full series of high-quality radiographs for new patient limited, or referral exams.
description: Limited exams for new patients often underrepresent disease. High-quality in-house imaging is necessary for accurate diagnosis.

text: I always recommend a pano at new patient exams (around age 6–7+) and every three years thereafter, regardless of insurance coverage.
description: Panoramic imaging tracks growth, development, missing teeth, and pathology.

competency_name: Treatment Planning for Long Term Health
text: I always offer definitive restorative treatment (composite, crown, EXT) for lesions extending past the DEJ.
description: Once decay has progressed into dentin, monitoring alone is no longer appropriate. Definitive treatment is the standard of care.

competency_name: Treatment Planning for Long Term Health
text: I always offer both white and silver crown options when full-coverage restorations are indicated.
description: Families value choice and transparency on esthetics, durability, and outcomes. Equitable care means ensuring all families are informed of all options.

competency_name: Treatment Planning for Long Term Health
text: I always consider the need for space maintenance when a primary tooth is extracted.
description: Premature tooth loss can affect eruption and alignment. Space maintainers help prevent bigger issues down the road.

competency_name: Treatment Planning for Long Term Health
text: I always evaluate the need for an ortho referral around 7-8 and again around 12-13 - and an oral surgery referral for 3rds around 15-16
description: Early evaluation allows proactive planning and prevention of more complex issues.

text: I always sign my clinical notes at the chair before the patient leaves.
description: Timely documentation ensures accuracy, prevents backlogs, and protects clinical integrity.

text: I always send patient referrals at the chair before the patient leaves.
description: Immediate referrals reduce delays, confusion, and follow-up failures.

text: I always print prescriptions at the chair before the patient leaves.
description: This prevents missed medications and unnecessary callbacks.

text: I always complete sedation medication logs at the time of sedation.
description: Real-time documentation is critical for safety, compliance, and auditing.

text: I Always Complete Team and Administrative Requests Within 24 Hours
description:
I complete email- or staff-requested tasks—such as insurance narratives, 22-point sheets, parent follow-ups, or other documentation requests—within 24 hours.

Whenever possible, I aim for same-day completion so the team can continue moving patient care and scheduling forward without delay.

text: I always review radiographs using the AI overlay to ensure nothing is overlooked.
description: AI supports diagnostic accuracy and consistency, especially in complex cases.

text: I always show up on time, prepared, and positive for morning huddle
description:
I arrive on time for morning huddle, attend consistently, and participate in a way that supports team alignment and a positive start to the day.

Morning huddle is an opportunity to lead through presence, preparedness, and constructive engagement, helping the team anticipate the day’s needs and maintain strong workflow.

text: I always consider the trust impact on patients and my team when deciding to call in absent to work.
description: Absences affect patients, schedules, and team morale. Reliability is a leadership expectation.

text: I Always Give and Receive Feedback with Respect
description: Feedback is part of working as a team. The goal is always to help each other do our jobs well and keep the day running smoothly, while maintaining trust and respect.

text: I always allow RDAs to guide the flow of the day.
description:
I allow RDAs to guide the flow of the day and direct me to the next patient, trusting them to manage timing, readiness, and transitions between patients.

This allows every team member to focus on their role and do their job well.

text: I always allow the RDA to formally present the patient and guardian to me before diving into the exam/treatment
description:
I pause and allow the RDA to formally present the patient and guardian at the chair for both new patient and recall exams before beginning my evaluation.

The RDA presentation provides the key clinical details so we can move smoothly from room to room while staying aligned as a team.

text: I always trust the RDA to provide clear and appropriate post-operative instructions.
description: RDAs are trained to deliver routine post-op instructions consistently. Delegating allows doctors to focus on reassurance and next steps.

text: I Always Warmly Greet the Family and Introduce Myself by Name
description:
I always pause, make eye contact, warmly greet the child and parent, and introduce myself by name when entering the room, especially when meeting a family for the first time.

I also acknowledge and thank the RDA for the introduction to reinforce teamwork in front of the family.

text: I Always Project a Calm and Confident Presence
description: Parents and children often mirror the doctor emotional state. Calm, aligned presence supports comprehension and trust.

text: I Always Ask “Tell Me More” When a Parent Hesitates on Treatment
description:
When a parent hesitates or declines recommended treatment, I begin the conversation with curiosity and listening, seeking to understand their concerns before responding.

If concerns persist after discussion, I clearly explain our standards of care and clinical recommendations, and establish clear, respectful boundaries when a parent’s requests for care repeatedly fall outside those standards.

text: I always promptly loop in my office manager, regional manager, or clinical director when a team member or system issue prevents me from practicing according to our standards of care.
description: When a team or system issue prevents me from practicing according to our standards of care, I promptly loop in my office manager, regional manager, or Clinical Director so the issue can be addressed appropriately.

text: I always ask parents "what matters most to you about your child's dental care and the experience they have with us"- Before Discussing Treatment Options
description:
When discussing treatment recommendations—especially when there are areas of concern—I ask parents what matters most to them about their child’s dental care and experience before presenting options.

This helps ensure the conversation is aligned with the family’s priorities and allows recommendations to be framed in a way that feels collaborative and thoughtful.

text: I always align treatment recommendations with what the family identifies as most important.
description: When families hear their priorities reflected back, trust increases and resistance decreases.

text: I always recommend sedation options based on what is safest and most likely to succeed for the child, while also considering what matters most to the family.
description:
I recommend sedation options based on what is safest and most likely to succeed for the child, while also considering what matters most to the family.

I begin with a clear professional recommendation and explanation, and then discuss other clinically appropriate options if families would like to explore them.

text: I always perform a brief pre-treatment check-in with the parent to confirm the plan, set expectations, and reinforce our commitment to the child’s comfort before beginning care.
description:
At the beginning of treatment appointments, I perform a brief check-in with the parent to confirm the plan, set expectations, and reinforce our commitment to the child’s comfort before beginning care.

This conversation is concise—typically 1–2 minutes—and ensures families understand the plan for the visit and any reasonable variations that could occur during treatment.

text: I always ensure a clear (mutually agreed upon) treatment plan is in place before leaving the room/conversation with parent and RDA.
description: While options may be discussed verbally, I direct the RDA to chart one clear treatment plan so the team and family leave with a shared understanding of what will happen next.

text: I always honor the existing treatment and sedation plan whenever possible
description:
When a patient is seen by a different provider, I carefully review the existing treatment and sedation plan and work to honor that plan whenever it remains clinically appropriate.

Before modifying a previously discussed or agreed-upon plan, I pause to consider the trust impact on the family and the alignment between providers, and ensure that any change is truly clinically necessary.

text: I always introduce age-appropriate future recommendations early so families understand what to expect as their child grows.
description:
I introduce age-appropriate future recommendations early so families understand what to expect as their child grows.

This helps normalize future care milestones and ensures recommendations feel planned and intentional, rather than sudden or reactive.
